title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 820–822 (Night 177, continuing nights-176), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 177 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. The jinniya Maymūna, daughter of al-Dimiryāṭ, one of the famous kings of the jinn, rises from the old Roman well at the first third of the night to go and eavesdrop on heaven, and sees a light burning in the tower where none has burned before. She follows it into the hall, finds the servant asleep at the door and on the couch a sleeping figure, a candle at his head and a lantern at his feet; she lifts the sheet from Qamar al-Zamān's face and stands stunned at his beauty, and the narrator gives two lines of verse on it. Being one of the believing jinn, she praises God, resolves that no one shall harm him, wonders how his family could leave him in that ruined place, kisses him between the eyes, covers him again and flies up toward the lowest heaven. There she hears the beating of wings, swoops on the ifrit Dahnash like a sparrowhawk, and he, terrified, adjures her by the Greatest Name and the seal of Solomon to spare him. She will not let him go until he says where he has come from; he says from the farthest lands of China, with a marvel he saw that very night, and asks for a written deed of freedom if his tale proves true. She threatens to pluck his feathers, tear his skin and break his bones if he lies; he accepts the condition — and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ السَّابِعَةُ وَالسَّبْعُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-sābiʿatu wa-al-sabʿūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the seventh and the seventy after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and seventy-seventh night,
sentences.n: The formula as before, with al-sābiʿa, “the seventh”, feminine to agree with layla.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ اسْمَ تِلْكَ الْجِنِّيَّةِ مَيْمُونَةُ ابْنَةُ الدِّمِرْيَاطِ أَحَدِ مُلُوكِ الْجَانِّ الْمَشْهُورِينَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna isma tilka al-jinniyyati Maymūnatu ibnatu al-Dimiryāṭi aḥadi mulūki al-jānni al-mashhūrīna
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that (the) name (of) that the-jinniya (was) Maymūna, daughter (of) al-Dimiryāṭ, one (of the) kings (of) the-jinn the-famous.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the name of that jinniya was Maymūna, daughter of al-Dimiryāṭ, one of the famous kings of the jinn.
sentences.n: Shahrazād opens by repeating the last words of the previous night. anna puts its noun ism, “name”, in the accusative; the predicate Maymūnatu stays nominative. This time the print sets the father's name as one word, الدمرياط, where last night it was split in two; it is the same name, and its vocalisation is still a guess. The shadda of الجنّية is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا اسْتَمَرَّ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ نَائِمًا إِلَى ثُلُثِ اللَّيْلِ الْأَوَّلِ طَلَعَتْ تِلْكَ الْعِفْرِيتَةُ مِنَ الْبِئْرِ الرُّومَانِيِّ وَقَصَدَتِ السَّمَاءَ لِاسْتِرَاقِ السَّمْعِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā istamarra Qamaru al-Zamāni nāʾiman ilā thuluthi al-layli al-awwali ṭalaʿat tilka al-ʿifrītatu mina al-biʾri al-rūmāniyyi wa-qaṣadati al-samāʾa li-istirāqi al-samʿi
sentences.l: And-when continued Qamar al-Zamān sleeping until (the) third (of) the-night, the-first, came-up that the-she-ifrit from the-well the-Roman and-made-for the-sky for-(the)-stealing (of) the-hearing.
sentences.i: And when Qamar al-Zamān had slept on until the first third of the night was over, that she-ifrit came up out of the Roman well and made for the sky, to eavesdrop on heaven.
sentences.n: istamarra, Form X of marra, “to go on, continue”, takes its predicate in the accusative, nāʾiman, “(continued) sleeping”; its shadda is printed. al-awwali, “the first”, agrees with thuluth, “third”, not with layl: “the first third of the night”. The jinniya of the last night is now called ʿifrīta, the feminine of ʿifrīt. istirāq al-samʿ, the verbal noun of istaraqa, Form VIII of saraqa, “to steal”, literally “the stealing of hearing”, is the Qurʾānic picture of the jinn creeping up to the lowest heaven to overhear the angels (Q 15:18, 72:8–9); li-, “for”, marks the purpose. The hamza of البئر and نائما is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا صَارَتْ فِي أَعْلَى الْبِئْرِ رَأَتْ نُورًا يَشْتَعِلُ فِى الْبُرْجِ عَلَى خِلَافِ الْعَادَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ṣārat fī aʿlā al-biʾri raʾat nūran yashtaʿilu fī al-burji ʿalā khilāfi al-ʿādati
sentences.l: And-when she-came-to-be in (the) top (of) the-well, she-saw a-light blazing in the-tower against (the) contrary (of) the-custom.
sentences.i: When she reached the top of the well, she saw a light burning in the tower, which was not the way of things there.
sentences.n: ṣāra fī, “to come to be in”, is simply “to reach”. yashtaʿilu, “blazing, burning”, is a clause describing the indefinite nūran, so no relative word is needed. The print spells the first fī with a dotted yāʾ and the second with alif maqṣūra, فى; it is the same word. ʿalā khilāfi al-ʿāda, “contrary to custom”: there was not usually a light there. The hamza of رأت is printed.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ تِلْكَ الْعِفْرِيتَةُ مُقِيمَةً فِي ذٰلِكَ الْمَكَانِ مُدَّةً مَدِيدَةً مِنَ السِّنِينَ فَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا أَنَا مَا عَهِدْتُ هُنَا شَيْأً مِنْ ذٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat tilka al-ʿifrītatu muqīmatan fī dhālika al-makāni muddatan madīdatan mina al-sinīna fa-qālat fī nafsihā anā mā ʿahidtu hunā shayʾan min dhālika
sentences.l: And-was that the-she-ifrit dwelling in that the-place a-span long of the-years, and-she-said in herself: I, not I-have-known here a-thing of that.
sentences.i: That she-ifrit had lived in that place for many long years, and she said to herself, “I have never known anything of the kind here.”
sentences.n: muddatan madīdatan, “a long span”, pairs two words of the same root, madda, “to stretch”, a favourite jingle. qālat fī nafsihā, “she said in herself”, is “she said to herself”, thought rather than speech. anā mā ʿahidtu: the pronoun put first for emphasis, then mā denying the perfect; ʿahida is “to know by experience, be used to”. shayʾan is printed شيأ, with the hamza on the alif of the accusative and no yāʾ seat, where Classical writes شيئا; it is the edition's spelling and kept.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتِ النُّورَ تَعَجَّبَتْ مِنْ هٰذَا الْأَمْرِ غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ وَخَطَرَ بِبَالِهَا أَنَّهُ لَابُدَّ لِذٰلِكَ مِنْ سَبَبٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾati al-nūra taʿajjabat min hādhā al-amri ghāyata al-ʿajabi wa-khaṭara bi-bālihā annahu lā budda li-dhālika min sababin
sentences.l: And-when she-saw the-light, she-wondered at this the-matter (the) utmost (of) the-wonder, and-it-occurred in-her-mind that-it (is): no escape for-that from a-cause.
sentences.i: When she saw the light she was astonished beyond measure, and it came to her mind that there must be some reason for it.
sentences.n: ghāyata al-ʿajab, “the utmost of wonder”, is an accusative of degree after taʿajjabat, “she wondered”. khaṭara bi-bālihi, “it crossed his mind”: bi- is “in”, bāl “mind”. annahu, “that it (is)”, carries a pronoun of the fact, introducing the clause lā budda li-X min Y, “X must have Y”, literally “there is no escape for X from Y”. The print sets لابدّ as one word, with its shadda; the hamza of رأت is printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَصَدَتْ نَاحِيَةَ ذٰلِكَ النُّورِ فَوَجَدَتْهُ خَارِجًا مِنَ الْقَاعَةِ فَدَخَلَتْ إِلَيْهَا فَوَجَدَتِ الْخَادِمَ نَائِمًا عَلَى بَابِ الْقَاعَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma qaṣadat nāḥiyata dhālika al-nūri fa-wajadathu khārijan mina al-qāʿati fa-dakhalat ilayhā fa-wajadati al-khādima nāʾiman ʿalā bābi al-qāʿati
sentences.l: Then she-made-for (the) direction (of) that the-light and-found-it coming-out from the-hall; and-she-entered to-it and-found the-servant sleeping at (the) door (of) the-hall.
sentences.i: Then she made toward that light and found it was coming from the hall; so she went in, and found the servant asleep at the door of the hall.
sentences.n: nāḥiyata, “(in the) direction (of)”, an accusative of place after qaṣadat. wajada, “to find”, takes two accusatives, the thing and what it is found to be: wajadathu khārijan, “found it coming out”, wajadati al-khādima nāʾiman, “found the servant sleeping”. dakhala ilā, “to go in to”. The servant is the one set to sleep at the door. The hamza of نائما is printed.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا دَخَلَتِ الْقَاعَةَ وَجَدَتْ سَرِيرًا مَنْصُوبًا وَعَلَيْهِ هَيْئَةُ إِنْسَانٍ نَائِمٍ وَشَمْعَةٌ مَوْقُودَةٌ عِنْدَ رَأْسِهِ وَفَانُوسٌ مَوْقُودٌ عِنْدَ رِجْلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā dakhalati al-qāʿata wajadat sarīran manṣūban wa-ʿalayhi hayʾatu insānin nāʾimin wa-shamʿatun mawqūdatun ʿinda raʾsihi wa-fānūsun mawqūdun ʿinda rijlayhi
sentences.l: And-when she-entered the-hall, she-found a-bed set-up, and-on-it (the) form (of) a-human sleeping, and-a-candle lit at his-head, and-a-lantern lit at his-two-feet.
sentences.i: When she entered the hall she found a bed set up, and on it the form of someone asleep, with a lit candle at his head and a lit lantern at his feet.
sentences.n: wa-ʿalayhi …, “and on it …”, is a circumstantial clause opened by wa-: a nominal sentence with the place first and the indefinite subjects after it. hayʾa is “shape, form”: she sees at first only a sleeping figure. mawqūd, “lit, kindled”, is the passive participle of waqada, feminine with shamʿa, masculine with fānūs. rijlayhi is the genitive dual, “his two feet”. The hamza of هيئة, نائم and رأسه is printed.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَتِ الْعِفْرِيتَةُ مَيْمُونَةُ مِنْ ذٰلِكَ النُّورِ وَتَقَدَّمَتْ إِلَيْهِ قَلِيلًا قَلِيلًا وَأَرْخَتْ أَجْنِحَتَهَا وَوَقَفَتْ عَلَى السَّرِيرِ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjabati al-ʿifrītatu Maymūnatu min dhālika al-nūri wa-taqaddamat ilayhi qalīlan qalīlan wa-arkhat ajniḥatahā wa-waqafat ʿalā al-sarīri
sentences.l: And-wondered the-she-ifrit Maymūna at that the-light, and-advanced to-it little little, and-let-down her-wings, and-stood at the-bed.
sentences.i: The she-ifrit Maymūna marvelled at that light, and drew near it little by little; she let down her wings and stood over the bed.
sentences.n: qalīlan qalīlan, “little by little”, the adverb doubled. arkhat, Form IV of rakhiya, “to loosen, let hang”: she lowers and folds her wings as she alights. ajniḥa is the plural of janāḥ, “wing”. waqafa ʿalā is “to stand over, beside”, here at the bedside rather than on it. The shadda of تقدّمت is printed.

sentences.t: وَكَشَفَتِ الْمُلَاءَةَ عَنْ وَجْهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَنَظَرَتْ إِلَيْهِ فَبُهِتَتْ فِي حُسْنِهِ وَجَمَالِهِ سَاعَةً زَمَانِيَّةً
sentences.tr: wa-kashafati al-mulāʾata ʿan wajhi Qamari al-Zamāni wa-naẓarat ilayhi fa-buhitat fī ḥusnihi wa-jamālihi sāʿatan zamāniyyatan
sentences.l: And-she-uncovered the-sheet from (the) face (of) Qamar al-Zamān, and-looked at-him, and-was-dumbstruck in his-comeliness and-his-beauty an-hour of-time.
sentences.i: She drew the sheet back from Qamar al-Zamān's face and looked at him, and stood dumbstruck at his comeliness and beauty for a good while.
sentences.n: kashafa X ʿan Y, “to uncover Y by taking X off it”: ʿan marks what is laid bare. buhita, passive in form, “to be struck dumb, confounded”; fī marks what dumbfounds her. ḥusn and jamāl, “comeliness and beauty”, are the stock pair. sāʿatan zamāniyyatan, “an hour of time”, is a stock phrase for a good while. The hamza of الملاءة is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ وَجَدَتْ ضَوْءَ وَجْهِهِ غَالِبًا عَلَى نُورِ الشَّمْعَةِ فَصَارَ وَجْهُهُ يَتَلَأْلَأُ نُورًا
sentences.tr: wa-qad wajadat ḍawʾa wajhihi ghāliban ʿalā nūri al-shamʿati fa-ṣāra wajhuhu yatalaʾlaʾu nūran
sentences.l: And-indeed she-found (the) brightness (of) his-face overcoming over (the) light (of) the-candle, and-became his-face glittering (in) light.
sentences.i: She found that the brightness of his face outshone the light of the candle, and his face was glittering with light.
sentences.n: wajada again with two accusatives: ḍawʾa wajhihi, “the brightness of his face”, and ghāliban ʿalā, “overcoming, prevailing over”. yatalaʾlaʾu, a quadriliteral verb, “to glitter, sparkle”, stands as the predicate of ṣāra; nūran, “in light”, is an accusative of specification. The hamzas of ضوء and يتلألأ are printed.

sentences.t: وَتَغَازَلَتْ مِنَ النَّوْمِ عَيْنَاهُ وَاسْوَدَّتْ مُقْلَتَاهُ وَاحْمَرَّ خَدَّاهُ وَفَتَرَ جَفْنَاهُ وَتَقَوَّسَ حَاجِبَاهُ وَفَاحَ مِسْكُهُ الْعَاطِرُ كَمَا قَالَ فِيهِ الشَّاعِرُ
sentences.tr: wa-taghāzalat mina al-nawmi ʿaynāhu wa-iswaddat muqlatāhu wa-iḥmarra khaddāhu wa-fatara jafnāhu wa-taqawwasa ḥājibāhu wa-fāḥa miskuhu al-ʿāṭiru kamā qāla fīhi al-shāʿiru
sentences.l: And-flirted from the-sleep his-two-eyes, and-blackened his-two-eyeballs, and-reddened his-two-cheeks, and-drooped his-two-eyelids, and-arched his-two-eyebrows, and-spread his-musk the-fragrant, as said about-him the-poet:
sentences.i: His eyes were languid and coquettish with sleep, the dark of his eyes grew darker, his cheeks flushed red, his eyelids drooped, his brows were arched like bows, and his fragrant musk spread abroad, as the poet said of him:
sentences.n: A run of rhyme in the dual ending -āhu, “his two …”: ʿaynāhu, muqlatāhu, khaddāhu, jafnāhu, ḥājibāhu. Each verb comes first and so stays singular before its dual subject, feminine for ʿayn and muqla, masculine for the rest. taghāzala, Form VI of the root of ghazal, “love talk”, is “to flirt”: the eyes, heavy with sleep, look as if they flirted. iswadda and iḥmarra are Form IX, the form for colours: “to grow black”, “to grow red”. muqla is the eyeball, especially its dark part. taqawwasa, “to bend like a bow (qaws)”. The shaddas of اسودّت، احمرّ، خدّاه and تقوّس are printed.

sentences.t:
قَبَّلْتُهُ فَاسْوَدَّتِ الْمُقلُ الَّتِيْ * هِيَ فِتْنَتِي وَاحْمَرَّتِ الْوَجَنَاتُ
يَا قَلْبُ اِنْ زَعَمَ الْعَوَاذِلُ اَنَّهُ * فِي الْحُسْنِ يُوْجَدُ مِثْلُهُ قُلْ هَاتُوْا
sentences.tr:
qabbaltuhu fa-iswaddati al-muqalu allatī * hiya fitnatī wa-iḥmarrati al-wajanātu
yā qalbu in zaʿama al-ʿawādhilu annahu * fī al-ḥusni yūjadu mithluhu qul hātū
sentences.l:
I-kissed-him, and-blackened the-eyeballs which * they (are) my-enthralment, and-reddened the-cheeks.
O heart, if claim the-censurers that-it * in the-beauty is-found his-like, say: Bring-(him)!
sentences.i:
I kissed him, and the eyes that are my undoing grew darker, and the cheeks flushed red.
O heart, if the censurers claim that his equal in beauty is to be found, say: Then produce him!
sentences.n: Two lines in the kāmil metre, picking up the prose's iswaddat and iḥmarra: the beloved darkens and blushes at the kiss. al-muqal is the plural of muqla, “eyeball”; fitna, “temptation, enthralment”, is what the eyes work on the lover. al-ʿawādhil, “the censurers”, are the stock blamers of love poetry. annahu, “that it (is so)”, again carries a pronoun of the fact before its clause. hātū, “bring (him)!”, plural imperative, is a dare: produce his equal if you can. The marks are the print's, copied as they stand, including the sukūn it puts on long vowels (الّتيْ, يوْجد, هاتوْا), the vowel on bare alif with no hamza sign (اِنْ, اَنّه), and the unmarked qāf of المقل.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ الْعِفْرِيتَةُ مَيْمُونَةُ بِنْتُ الدِّمِرْيَاطِ سَبَّحَتِ اللَّهَ وَقَالَتْ تَبَارَكَ اللَّهُ أَحْسَنُ الْخَالِقِينَ وَكَانَتْ تِلْكَ الْعِفْرِيتَةُ مِنَ الْجِنِّ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾathu al-ʿifrītatu Maymūnatu bintu al-Dimiryāṭi sabbaḥati allāha wa-qālat tabāraka allāhu aḥsanu al-khāliqīna wa-kānat tilka al-ʿifrītatu mina al-jinni al-muʾminīna
sentences.l: And-when saw-him the-she-ifrit Maymūna, daughter (of) al-Dimiryāṭ, she-glorified God and-said: Blessed-is God, (the) best (of) the-creators! And-was that the-she-ifrit of the-jinn the-believing.
sentences.i: When the she-ifrit Maymūna, daughter of al-Dimiryāṭ, saw him, she glorified God and said, “Blessed be God, the best of creators!” For that she-ifrit was one of the believing jinn.
sentences.n: sabbaḥa, Form II, “to glorify God”, that is, to say subḥāna allāh; its shadda is printed. tabāraka allāhu aḥsanu al-khāliqīna is a verse of the Qurʾān (23:14), said at the sight of a beautiful creature. Here her father is introduced with bint, “daughter”, where above it was ibna; the two are the same. The Qurʾān speaks of jinn who heard it and believed (sura 72), and Maymūna is one of these: hence her piety, and her care for the youth. The hamza of رأته and المؤمنين is printed.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَمَرَّتْ سَاعَةً وَهِيَ تَنْظُرُ إِلَى وَجْهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ وَتُوَحِّدُ اللَّهَ وَتَغْبِطُهُ عَلَى حُسْنِهِ وَجَمَالِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-istamarrat sāʿatan wa-hiya tanẓuru ilā wajhi Qamari al-Zamāni wa-tuwaḥḥidu allāha wa-taghbiṭuhu ʿalā ḥusnihi wa-jamālihi
sentences.l: And-she-continued an-hour, and-she looking at (the) face (of) Qamar al-Zamān, and-professing-(the)-oneness (of) God, and-envying-him for his-comeliness and-his-beauty.
sentences.i: She remained a while gazing at Qamar al-Zamān's face, proclaiming the oneness of God and envying him his comeliness and beauty.
sentences.n: wa-hiya tanẓuru …, “she looking …”, is a circumstantial clause with wa- and a pronoun. tuwaḥḥidu, Form II of waḥada, “to declare one”, is to profess that God is one, saying lā ilāha illā allāh. ghabaṭa, “to envy”, in the harmless sense: to wish for oneself what another has, without wishing him to lose it; ʿalā marks what is envied. The shadda of فاستمرّت and the damma and shadda of تُوحّد are printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا وَاللَّهِ إِنِّي لَمْ أَضُرَّهُ وَلَمْ أَتْرُكْ أَحَدًا يُؤْذِيهِ وَمِنْ كُلِّ سُوءٍ أَفْدِيهِ فَإِنَّ هٰذَا الْوَجْهَ الْمَلِيحَ لَا يَسْتَحِقُّ إِلَّا النَّظَرَ إِلَيْهِ وَالتَّسْبِيحَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat fī nafsihā wa-allāhi innī lam aḍurrahu wa-lam atruk aḥadan yuʾdhīhi wa-min kulli sūʾin afdīhi fa-inna hādhā al-wajha al-malīḥa lā yastaḥiqqu illā al-naẓara ilayhi wa-al-tasbīḥa ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And-she-said in herself: By-God, I not I-harmed-him, and-not I-left anyone harming-him, and-from every evil I-ransom-him; for this the-face the-lovely not deserves except the-looking at-it and-the-glorifying over-it.
sentences.i: And she said to herself, “By God, I will not harm him, nor let anyone hurt him, and from every evil I will shield him with my life; for this lovely face deserves nothing but to be gazed upon, and God glorified for it.
sentences.n: lam with the jussive denies the past, “I did not harm”, but here, under the oath wa-allāhi, it is a vow for the future, “I will not harm”, where Classical would say lan aḍurrahu; the colloquial way of swearing is kept as printed. aḍurrahu is the jussive of the doubled verb ḍarra, its shadda printed. afdīhi, “I ransom him”, is “I would give myself for him”; it rhymes with yuʾdhīhi, and ilayhi with ʿalayhi, sajʿ in her speech. al-tasbīḥ ʿalayhi, “glorifying (God) over it”, saying subḥāna allāh at the sight of it. The shadda of الّا is printed; the hamza of يؤذيه is printed.

sentences.t: وَلٰكِنْ كَيْفَ هَانَ عَلَى أَهْلِهِ حَتَّى أَنَّهُمْ حَطُّوهُ فِي هٰذَا الْمَكَانِ الْخَرَابِ
sentences.tr: wa-lākin kayfa hāna ʿalā ahlihi ḥattā annahum ḥaṭṭūhu fī hādhā al-makāni al-kharābi
sentences.l: But how was-he-of-little-account to his-family, so-far that they put-him in this the-place the-ruin?
sentences.i: But how could his people hold him so cheap that they put him away in this ruined place?
sentences.n: hāna ʿalā, “to be of little account to, be held cheap by”. ḥattā annahum, “so that they (even) …”: ḥattā followed by anna is a loose, non-Classical joining, where Classical would say ḥattā ḥaṭṭūhu. ḥaṭṭa, “to put down, set”, is the everyday word for “to put”; its shadda is printed. al-kharāb, “ruin”, is a noun used here as an adjective, “the ruined place”. lākin is spelled without its alif, as always, and pointed with the small upright alif.

sentences.t: فَلَوْ طَلَعَ لَهُ أَحَدٌ مِنْ مَرَدَتِنَا فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ لَعَطِبَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-law ṭalaʿa lahu aḥadun min maradatinā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati la-ʿaṭibahu
sentences.l: For-if came-up to-him one of our-rebels in this the-hour, surely-he-would-have-destroyed-him.
sentences.i: For if one of our rebel jinn were to come upon him at this hour, he would surely destroy him.
sentences.n: law, “if”, of a supposed case, with the perfect; its answer, la-ʿaṭibahu, “he would surely have destroyed him”, takes the la- that marks the answer of law. Classical ʿaṭiba is intransitive, “to perish”; here it takes an object, “to ruin, destroy”, as in the later language, and that use is kept as printed. ṭalaʿa li-, “to come up to, come upon”: li- marks the one met. marada is the plural of mārid, “rebellious”, the jinn who defy God, as against the believers like Maymūna; the print points the word, مَرَدَتِنا, and its vowels are kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ تِلْكَ الْعِفْرِيتَةَ مَالَتْ عَلَيْهِ وَقَبَّلَتْهُ بَيْنَ عَيْنَيْهِ وَبَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ أَرْخَتِ الْمُلَاءَةَ عَلَى وَجْهِهِ وَغَطَّتْهُ بِهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna tilka al-ʿifrītata mālat ʿalayhi wa-qabbalathu bayna ʿaynayhi wa-baʿda dhālika arkhati al-mulāʾata ʿalā wajhihi wa-ghaṭṭathu bihā
sentences.l: Then (indeed) that the-she-ifrit leaned over-him and-kissed-him between his-two-eyes; and-after that she-let-down the-sheet over his-face and-covered-him with-it.
sentences.i: Then the she-ifrit bent over him and kissed him between the eyes; after that she let the sheet down over his face and covered him with it.
sentences.n: thumma inna, “then indeed”, the narrator's usual way of moving the story on: inna puts tilka al-ʿifrītata in the accusative, and the verb mālat follows as its predicate. māla ʿalā, “to lean over, bend down to”. arkhā, Form IV, “to let hang, let down”; its final vowel is a kasra here only to join it to al-mulāʾata. mulāʾa, a sheet or wrap; the ء is printed, as are the shaddas of قبّلته and غطّته. ghaṭṭā bi-, “to cover with”: bi- marks the covering.

sentences.t: وَفَتَحَتْ أَجْنِحَتَهَا وَطَارَتْ نَاحِيَةَ السَّمَاءِ وَطَلَعَتْ مِنْ دَوْرِ تِلْكَ الْقَاعَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-fataḥat ajniḥatahā wa-ṭārat nāḥiyata al-samāʾi wa-ṭalaʿat min dawri tilka al-qāʿati
sentences.l: And-she-opened her-wings and-flew (in the) direction (of) the-sky, and-went-up out-of (the) storey (of) that the-hall.
sentences.i: She spread her wings and flew off towards the sky, rising up out of that hall.
sentences.n: nāḥiyata, “side, direction”, in the accusative used as an adverb: “towards the sky”. ṭalaʿa min, “to go up out of, come out of”. dawr is in the later language “storey, floor” of a building, so min dawri tilka al-qāʿati is probably “out of the storey of that hall”, up through the top of the tower; the phrase is not quite clear, and “out of the round of that hall” is also possible.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ تَزَلْ طَائِرَةً فِى الْهَوَاءِ وَصَاعِدَةً فِى الْجَوِّ إِلَى أَنْ قَرُبَتْ مِنْ سَمَاءِ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: wa-lam tazal ṭāʾiratan fī al-hawāʾi wa-ṣāʿidatan fī al-jawwi ilā an qarubat min samāʾi al-dunyā
sentences.l: And-not she-ceased flying in the-air and-rising in the-sky, until that she-drew-near to (the) heaven (of) the-near-world.
sentences.i: She went on flying through the air and climbing the sky until she came close to the lowest heaven.
sentences.n: lam tazal, “she did not cease”, with two predicates in the accusative, ṭāʾiratan … wa-ṣāʿidatan, “flying … and rising”, as lam yazal nāʾiman last night. The halves pair off, fī al-hawāʾi / fī al-jawwi. ilā an + perfect, “until”. samāʾ al-dunyā, “the heaven of the near world”, is the lowest of the seven heavens, the one nearest the earth, up to which the jinn rise. The ئ of طائرة and the shadda of الجوّ are printed; the print writes في as فى here.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِهَا سَمِعَتْ خَفْقَ أَجْنِحَةٍ طَائِرَةٍ فِى الْهَوَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bihā samiʿat khafqa ajniḥatin ṭāʾiratin fī al-hawāʾi
sentences.l: And-behold, (there was) she: she-heard (the) beating (of) wings flying in the-air.
sentences.i: And all at once she heard the beat of wings flying through the air.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bihā, “and behold, her”: idhā of surprise, with bi- marking the one caught in the moment. Here a full verb follows, samiʿat, “she heard”, a loose turn of the later language; Classical would say simply fa-samiʿat or wa-idhā hiya tasmaʿu. khafq, “beating, flapping (of wings)”. ṭāʾira, “flying”, is feminine singular to agree with the plural ajniḥa, “wings”.

sentences.t: فَقَصَدَتْ نَاحِيَةَ تِلْكَ الْأَجْنِحَةِ فَدَنَتْ مِنْهَا فَوَجَدَتْهُ عِفْرِيتًا يُقَالُ لَهُ دَهْنَشُ فَانْقَضَّتْ عَلَيْهِ انْقِضَاضَ الْبَاشِقِ
sentences.tr: fa-qaṣadat nāḥiyata tilka al-ajniḥati fa-danat minhā fa-wajadathu ʿifrītan yuqālu lahu Dahnashu fa-inqaḍḍat ʿalayhi inqiḍāḍa al-bāshiqi
sentences.l: And-she-made-for (the) direction (of) those the-wings, and-drew-near to-them, and-found-him an-ifrit (of whom) it-is-said to-him Dahnash; and-she-swooped upon-him (the) swooping (of) the-sparrowhawk.
sentences.i: She made for the sound of those wings and drew near them, and found it was an ifrit named Dahnash; and she swooped down on him as a sparrowhawk swoops.
sentences.n: fa-wajadathu ʿifrītan, “and she found him an ʿifrīt”: the pronoun -hu, “him”, stands for the owner of the wings before he is named, and ʿifrītan is the second object of wajada, “found (to be)”. yuqālu lahu, “it is said to him”, the usual way of saying “who was called”. Dahnash is the ʿifrīt's name; his father's, Shamhūrash, comes at the end of the night. inqiḍāḍa al-bāshiqi: the verbal noun of the verb just used, inqaḍḍa, “to swoop”, set after it as an absolute object, “she swooped the swoop of the sparrowhawk”, that is, like a sparrowhawk. bāshiq, a small hawk. The shadda of انقضّت is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَحَسَّ بِهَا دَهْنَشُ وَعَرَفَ أَنَّهَا مَيْمُونَةُ بِنْتُ مَلِكِ الْجِنِّ خَافَ مِنْهَا وَارْتَعَدَتْ فَرَائِصُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aḥassa bihā Dahnashu wa-ʿarafa annahā Maymūnatu bintu maliki al-jinni khāfa minhā wa-irtaʿadat farāʾiṣuhu
sentences.l: And-when sensed her Dahnash, and-knew that-she (was) Maymūna, daughter (of the) king (of) the-jinn, he-feared (from) her, and-quivered his-shoulder-flesh.
sentences.i: When Dahnash became aware of her and knew her for Maymūna, daughter of the king of the jinn, he was afraid of her and shook in every limb.
sentences.n: aḥassa bi-, “to sense, become aware of”: the verb takes its object with bi-. Her father is al-Dimiryāṭ, named last night as one of the famous kings of the jinn. khāfa min, “to be afraid of”. farāʾiṣ is the plural of farīṣa, the flesh between the shoulder and the flank, which quivers in fear; irtaʿadat farāʾiṣuhu, “his shoulder-flesh shook”, is the stock phrase for terror. The shadda of احسّ and the ئ of فرائصه are printed.

sentences.t: فَاسْتَجَارَبِهَا وَقَالَ لَهَا أُقْسِمُ عَلَيْكِ بِالِاسْمِ الْأَعْظَمِ الْمُكَرَّمِ وَالطِّلَسْمِ الْأَكْرَمِ الْمَنْقُوشِ عَلَى خَاتَمِ سُلَيْمَانَ أَنْ تَرْفُقِي بِي وَلَا تُؤْذِينِي
sentences.tr: fa-istajāra bihā wa-qāla lahā uqsimu ʿalayki bi-al-ismi al-aʿẓami al-mukarrami wa-al-ṭilasmi al-akrami al-manqūshi ʿalā khātami Sulaymāna an tarfuqī bī wa-lā tuʾdhīnī
sentences.l: And-he-sought-protection with-her and-said to-her: I-adjure you by-the-Name the-Greatest, the-honoured, and-the-talisman the-most-noble, the-engraved upon (the) seal-ring (of) Solomon, that you-be-gentle with-me and-not harm-me.
sentences.i: He begged her protection and said to her, “I adjure you by the Greatest Name, the honoured, and by the noblest of talismans, the one engraved on Solomon's seal-ring, to be gentle with me and not hurt me.”
sentences.n: The print has انسم, a misprint for اقسم, corrected here. The print also runs fa-istajāra bihā together as one word, فاستجاربها, and that spacing is kept. istajāra bi-, Form X of jāra, “to seek someone's protection”: bi- marks the one appealed to. uqsimu ʿalayki bi-, “I adjure you by”: ʿalā marks the one put under the oath, bi- what is sworn by. al-ism al-aʿẓam, “the Greatest Name”, is the hidden name of God; Solomon's seal-ring is the ring by which he ruled the jinn. These are the strongest oaths that can be laid on a jinn, and the epithets rhyme, al-mukarram / al-akram. an tarfuqī … wa-lā tuʾdhīnī, subjunctives after an, with the -na of the feminine ending dropped; rafaqa bi-, “to be gentle with”, takes its object with bi-. The ؤ of تؤذيني is printed.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَتْ مَيْمُونَةُ مِنْ دَهْنَشَ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ حَنَّ قَلْبُهَا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿat Maymūnatu min Dahnasha hādhā al-kalāma ḥanna qalbuhā ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And-when heard Maymūna from Dahnash this the-speech, felt-tender her-heart toward-him.
sentences.i: When Maymūna heard these words from Dahnash, her heart softened towards him.
sentences.n: ḥanna ʿalā, “to feel tenderness or pity for”; the shadda of حنّ is printed. min Dahnasha: the name is treated as a diptote, so its genitive ends in -a.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لَهُ لَقَدْ أَقْسَمْتَ عَلَيَّ يَا مَلْعُونُ بِقَسَمٍ عَظِيمٍ وَلٰكِنْ لَا أُعْتِقُكَ حَتَّى تُخْبِرَنِي مِنْ أَيْنَ مَجِيئُكَ فِي هٰذِهِ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lahu la-qad aqsamta ʿalayya yā malʿūnu bi-qasamin ʿaẓīmin wa-lākin lā uʿtiquka ḥattā tukhbiranī min ayna majīʾuka fī hādhihi al-sāʿati
sentences.l: And-she-said to-him: Indeed you-have-adjured me, O accursed-one, by-an-oath mighty; but not I-free-you until you-tell-me from where (is) your-coming at this the-hour.
sentences.i: And she said to him, “You have adjured me by a mighty oath, accursed one; but I will not let you go until you tell me where you are coming from at this hour.”
sentences.n: la-qad + perfect, emphatic: “you have indeed …”. yā malʿūn, “O accursed one”, the usual way of addressing a jinn, even by one about to spare him. aʿtaqa, Form IV, “to set (a slave) free”: she speaks as an owner to a captive, and in a moment Dahnash will ask to be her ʿatīq, her freedman. ḥattā + subjunctive, “until”. min ayna majīʾuka, “from where is your coming”, a nominal sentence with no verb. The shadda of عليّ and the ئ of مجيئك are printed; here the print dots في.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا أَيُّهَا السَّيِّدَةُ اعْلَمِي أَنَّ مَجِيئِي مِنْ آخِرِ بِلَادِ الصِّينِ وَمِنْ دَاخِلِ الْجَزَائِرِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā ayyuhā al-sayyidatu iʿlamī anna majīʾī min ākhiri bilādi al-ṣīni wa-min dākhili al-jazāʾiri
sentences.l: And-he-said to-her: O the-lady, know that my-coming (is) from (the) farthest (of the) lands (of) the-China, and-from (the) inside (of) the-islands.
sentences.i: He said to her, “My lady, know that I come from the farthest lands of China, from deep within its islands.”
sentences.n: ayyuhā al-sayyidatu: Classical would have the feminine ayyatuhā with a woman, but ayyuhā for both genders is usual in the later language and in the Nights. ākhir, “last, farthest end”, with its madda printed. al-jazāʾir, “the islands”, with the ئ printed: the islands of the far east beyond China.

sentences.t: وَأُخْبِرُكِ بِأُعْجُوبَةٍ رَأَيْتُهَا فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ فَإِنْ وَجَدْتِ كَلَامِي صَحِيحًا فَاتْرُكِينِي أَرُوحُ إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِي
sentences.tr: wa-ukhbiruki bi-uʿjūbatin raʾaytuhā fī hādhihi al-laylati fa-in wajadti kalāmī ṣaḥīḥan fa-itrukīnī arūḥu ilā ḥāli sabīlī
sentences.l: And-I-tell-you of-a-wonder I-saw-it in this the-night; and-if you-find my-speech true, then-leave-me (that) I-go to (the) state (of) my-way.
sentences.i: “And I will tell you of a wonder I saw this night; and if you find that what I say is true, let me go on my way.”
sentences.n: The print has الميلة, a misprint for الليلة, corrected here. akhbara bi-, “to tell of”: the verb takes what is told with bi-. uʿjūba, “a wonder, a marvel”. wajada … ṣaḥīḥan, “to find (it) true”, with the second object in the accusative. fa-itrukīnī arūḥu, “leave me, I go”: rāḥa, “to go”, is the everyday verb of the later language, and the imperfect follows the command directly, without an, a colloquial turn. ilā ḥāli sabīlī, “to the state of my way”, that is, “about my business”. The أ of رأيتها is printed.

sentences.t: وَاكْتُبِي لِي بِخَطِّكِ وَثِيقَةً أَنِّي عَتِيقُكِ حَتَّى لَا يُعَارِضَنِي أَحَدٌ مِنْ أَرْهَاطِ الْجِنِّ الطَّيَّارَةِ الْعُلْوِيَّةِ وَالسُّفْلِيَّةِ وَالْغَوَّاصَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-uktubī lī bi-khaṭṭiki wathīqatan annī ʿatīquki ḥattā lā yuʿāriḍanī aḥadun min arhāṭi al-jinni al-ṭayyārati al-ʿulwiyyati wa-al-sufliyyati wa-al-ghawwāṣati
sentences.l: And-write for-me in-your-hand a-deed that-I (am) your-freedman, so-that not opposes-me anyone of (the) bands (of) the-jinn, the-flying, the-upper and-the-lower and-the-diving.
sentences.i: “And write me a deed in your own hand that I am your freedman, so that no one of the tribes of the jinn may stand in my way, whether they fly, or dwell above or below, or dive in the sea.”
sentences.n: wathīqa, a written deed, a warrant; ʿatīq, “freed slave, freedman”, one set free by his owner and still under her protection. ḥattā lā + subjunctive, “so that … not”. ʿāraḍa, Form III, “to oppose, stand in the way of”. arhāṭ is a plural of rahṭ, “band, clan”. The adjectives sort the jinn by their realms, al-ṭayyāra, “the flyers”, al-ʿulwiyya, “the upper”, al-sufliyya, “the lower”, al-ghawwāṣa, “the divers”; all are feminine singular, agreeing with the plural arhāṭ as broken plurals allow. The shadda of الطيّارة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ لَهُ مَيْمُونَةُ فَمَا الَّذِي رَأَيْتَهُ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ يَا كَذَّابُ يَا مَلْعُونُ فَأَخْبِرْنِي وَلَا تَكْذِبْ عَلَيَّ وَتُرِيدُأَنْ تَنْفَلِتَ مِنِّي بِكَذِبِكَ
sentences.tr: qālat lahu Maymūnatu fa-mā alladhī raʾaytahu fī hādhihi al-laylati yā kadhdhābu yā malʿūnu fa-akhbirnī wa-lā takdhib ʿalayya wa-turīdu an tanfalita minnī bi-kadhibika
sentences.l: Said to-him Maymūna: So-what (is) that-which you-saw-it in this the-night, O liar, O accursed-one? So-tell-me, and-not lie to-me, and-(you)-want to slip-away from-me by-your-lying.
sentences.i: Maymūna said to him, “Well, what did you see this night, you liar, you accursed one? Tell me, and do not lie to me, thinking to slip away from me with your lies.”
sentences.n: The print runs wa-turīdu an together as one word, وتريدان, and that spacing is kept. wa-turīdu an …, “and you want to …”: the wa- joins to the command the state she suspects him of, “do not lie to me, wanting to slip away”. infalata, Form VII, “to slip loose, get away”. kadhaba ʿalā, “to lie to”. kadhdhāb, “great liar”, an intensive form; its shadda is printed, as is that of عليّ. alladhī raʾaytahu, “that which you saw it”: the relative clause keeps a pronoun, -hu, pointing back to alladhī. The أ of رأيته is printed. qālat lahu Maymūnatu opens without wa- or fa-, as speech often does.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أُقْسِمُ بِحَقِّ النَّقْشِ الْمَكْتُوبِ عَلَى فَصِّ خَاتَمِ سُلَيْمَانَ بْنِ دَاؤُدَ عَلَيْهِمَا السَّلَامُ إِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ كَلَامُكَ صَحِيحًا نَتَفْتُ رِيشَكَ بِيَدِي وَمَزَّقْتُ جِلْدَكَ وَكَسَّرْتُ عَظْمَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-anā uqsimu bi-ḥaqqi al-naqshi al-maktūbi ʿalā faṣṣi khātami Sulaymāna ibni Dāwūda ʿalayhimā al-salāmu in lam yakun kalāmuka ṣaḥīḥan nataftu rīshaka bi-yadī wa-mazzaqtu jildaka wa-kassartu ʿaẓmaka
sentences.l: And-I, I-swear by (the) right (of) the-engraving the-written upon (the) stone (of the) seal-ring (of) Solomon son (of) David, upon-them-both (be) the-peace: if not is your-speech true, I-plucked your-feathers with-my-hand, and-tore your-skin, and-broke your-bone.
sentences.i: “And I swear by the virtue of the engraving written on the stone of the seal-ring of Solomon son of David, peace be upon them both, that if what you say is not true, I will pluck out your feathers with my own hand, tear your skin to pieces and break your bones.”
sentences.n: bi-ḥaqqi, “by the right of, by the virtue of”, the usual form of an oath by something holy. faṣṣ, the stone or bezel of a ring, which carries the engraving. ʿalayhimā al-salām, “peace be upon them both”, a dual blessing, since Solomon and David are both prophets in Islam. in lam yakun … nataftu: in the answer of a condition the perfect has future sense, “I will pluck”. Dahnash has feathers: the jinn of this tale fly on wings. mazzaqa and kassara, Form II intensives, “to tear to shreds”, “to smash”; ʿaẓm, “bone”, is singular for the whole skeleton. The shaddas of فصّ, مزّقت and كسّرت are printed, and so is the ؤ of داؤد, the edition's spelling of Dāwūd, David.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهَا الْعِفْرِيتُ دَهْنَشُ ابْنُ شَمْهُورَشَ الطَّيَّارُ رَضِيتُ يَا سَيِّدَتِى بِهٰذَا الشَّرْطِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahā al-ʿifrītu Dahnashu ibnu Shamhūrasha al-ṭayyāru raḍītu yā sayyidatī bi-hādhā al-sharṭi
sentences.l: And-said to-her the-ifrit Dahnash son (of) Shamhūrash, the-flyer: I-have-accepted, O my-lady, this the-condition.
sentences.i: Dahnash ibn Shamhūrash, the flying ifrit, said to her, “I accept this condition, my lady.”
sentences.n: Dahnash ibn Shamhūrash: the ʿifrīt now has his full name. Shamhūrash is a name of the jinn known from Arabic books of magic, where a Shamhūrash is a king of the jinn; the vocalisation of both names is uncertain. Here the print writes ابن with its alif between the two names, where a line earlier it had بن, and both are kept. al-ṭayyār, “the great flyer”, an intensive of ṭāra, “to fly”, in apposition to the ʿifrīt. raḍiya bi-, “to be content with, accept”: bi- marks what is accepted. The print writes سيدتي as سيدتى, and the shadda of الطيّار is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, here with its usual ʿan, “from”, where last night's print had min. Shahrazāda is the object, put before the subject al-ṣabāḥu, and the rhyme falls on al-ṣabāḥu / al-mubāḥi.
